source_text:
Fragmentum in illud: Gaudete in illa die [Sp.]
93.780 Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ σώματι ὁ ὑγιαίνων καὶ εὐσωματῶν, καὶ πρὸ τῆς τρυφῆς
αὐτῷ τούτῳ τρυφᾷ, συγκεκληρωμένην ἔχων τῇ ὑγείᾳ τὴν ἡδονὴν, καὶ οὔτε ἀέρων
αὐτὸν ἀνωμαλίαι, οὔτε αὐχμὸς οὔτε κρυμὸς, οὕτε εὐτέλεια τραπέζης, οὐκ ἄλλο τι
τῶν τοιούτων λυπῆσαι δύναιτ' ἂν, ἀρκούσης τῆς ὑγιείας τὴν ἐκ τούτων
διακρούσασθαι βλάβην, οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ψυχῆς συμβαίνειν εἴωθε· διὰ τοῦτο καὶ
Παῦλος μυρία πάσχων δεινὰ, ἔχαιρεν οὕτω λέγων· Χαίρω ἐν τοῖς παθήμασί μου
ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν οὐ μόνον ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν, ᾗ ἔπαθλον κεῖται τῆς ἀρετῆς,
ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ πάσχειν, ἐπεὶ καὶ τοῦτο μέγιστον ἔπαθλον, τὸ ὑπὲρ ἀληθείας τι
thought_title: Health and the pleasure of suffering for truth
orientation: Olympiodorus opens by comparing bodily health to spiritual health, then introduces Paul rejoicing in his sufferings.
pass_a_gloss: For just as in the body the one who is healthy and of good body, even before luxury, takes pleasure in this very thing, having pleasure allotted together with health, and neither irregularities of airs, nor drought, nor cold, nor cheapness of table, nor any other of such things could grieve him, since health is sufficient to beat away the harm from these things, so indeed also in the case of the soul it is accustomed to happen. Because of this Paul too, suffering countless terrible things, was rejoicing, saying thus: I rejoice in my sufferings for you, not only in the kingdom of heaven, in which a prize is set for virtue, but also in the very suffering, since this too is the greatest prize, to suffer something for the truth.

choices.why: Keeps the literal bodily sense of the compound, matching the physical analogy Olympiodorus is drawing.
The noun τρυφή is rendered 'luxury' to preserve the contrast with the verb τρυφάω, which is rendered 'takes pleasure' to show the same root in different grammatical roles.
Preserves the perfect passive participle's sense of a fixed, inherited share joined to health.
Keeps the forceful, defensive sense of the verb for warding off harm.
Literal rendering of the plural neuter adjective phrase, preserving the hyperbolic quantity and the severity.
Keeps the middle/passive sense of κεῖται as 'is laid down' or 'is set' for the prize.

bible_refs.note: Χαίρω ἐν τοῖς παθήμασί μου ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν

pass_b_english: Just as in the body, a person who is healthy and of good body takes pleasure even before luxury, having pleasure allotted together with health; and neither irregularities of the air, nor drought, nor cold, nor a cheap table, nor anything else of that kind could grieve such a person, since health is enough to beat away the harm from these things—so the same thing is accustomed to happen in the soul. For this reason Paul, though suffering countless terrible things, rejoiced, saying, "I rejoice in my sufferings for you..." [the quotation breaks off]—not only in the kingdom of heaven, in which a prize is set for virtue, but also in the very suffering, since this too is the greatest prize: to suffer something for the truth... [fragment breaks off]

problems.quote: saying: "I rejoice in my sufferings for you" (Colossians 1:24)
problems.source_quote: λέγων· Χαίρω ἐν τοῖς παθήμασί μου ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν
problems.why: The parenthetical citation (Colossians 1:24) is editorial addition not in source; more critically, the source quotation breaks off grammatically (no verb completion), but English presents it as a complete sentence with quotation marks, hiding the fragmentary nature marked by [Sp.] and voice note.
problems.fix: saying, "I rejoice in my sufferings for you..." [the quotation breaks off]
problems.ruling: Source ends mid-sentence at 'τι'; English closes quote, hiding fragmentary break-off. Misleads reader about text's state.

problems.quote: to suffer something for the truth
problems.why: The source breaks off at τι (incomplete: 'something...'), but English completes the thought with 'to suffer something for the truth', smoothing over the fragmentary nature.
problems.fix: to suffer something for the truth... [fragment breaks off]
problems.ruling: Source breaks off at 'τι' (incomplete); English 'to suffer something for the truth' supplies a verb, hiding fragmentary nature.

problems.why: Same Greek root (hedone/hedy) rendered 'pleasure' vs 'occasion of pleasure'—reader may miss connection.
problems.fix: Unify as 'pleasure' or 'delight' throughout.

problems.quote: a prize is set for virtue
problems.why: 'Prize' (brabeion) and 'crown' (stephanos) alternate as rewards; reader may not see they are parallel.
problems.fix: Use 'prize/crown' consistently or note equivalence.

problems.fix: 'a healthy, robust person takes pleasure even without luxury'

problems.why: 'Allotted together with' is awkward calque; not natural English.
problems.fix: 'having pleasure as part of health itself' or 'with health as its companion'

problems.why: Colossians 1:24 says 'I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake,' not 'for you'—minor but inaccurate.
problems.fix: Use standard translation: 'on your behalf' or 'for your sake'.

problems.fix: Reword: 'having pleasure as a natural accompaniment of health.'

problems.quote: a cheap table
problems.why: 'Cheap table' sounds modern; likely means plain or meager food.
problems.fix: Use 'meager fare' or 'plain food.'

problems.quote: beat away the harm
problems.why: 'Beat away' is an odd rendering; Greek likely means 'ward off' or 'repel.'
problems.fix: Use 'ward off' or 'repel.'

fixed: The Scripture reference to Colossians 1:24 is retained because the source text's wording closely echoes that verse, even though the exact phrase 'I rejoice in my sufferings for you' is not a direct quotation of the full verse; the reference is editorial and appropriate.
The speaker attribution issue is addressed by removing the parenthetical citation from the quotation and keeping the editorial marker that Paul's words break off and Olympiodorus resumes.

last_rejected.why: Glossary term 'health' not used; 'good body' misses the health analogy.
last_rejected.ruling: εὐσωματῶν means 'well-bodied/healthy'; 'of good body' is within normal range. No glossary error shown.

last_rejected.source_quote: λέγων· Χαίρω ἐν τοῖς παθήμασί μου ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν
last_rejected.why: The English suggests Paul breaks off, but the source shows Paul speaks and the author breaks off the quotation.
last_rejected.fix: saying, "I rejoice in my sufferings for you," [the author's quotation breaks off]
last_rejected.ruling: Brackets indicate the quotation breaks off; this is standard editorial notation, not a speaker attribution error.

last_rejected.quote: not only in the kingdom of heaven
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐ μόνον ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν
last_rejected.why: The 'not only' (οὐ μόνον) belongs to Paul's broken quotation, not the author's continuation; English misattributes it.
last_rejected.fix: saying, "I rejoice... for you, not only in the kingdom of heaven" [breaks off]—the author adds: not only... but also...
last_rejected.ruling: οὐ μόνον ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ follows the quotation; English correctly renders it as author's continuation with 'not only...but also' structure.
